claim: The Roman Empire is conventionally dated from 27 BCE (principate of Augustus).
Court chronicle links Chandragupta Maurya to the founding of the Maurya dynasty.
notes: Illustrative curated link; not an auto-generated inference.

claim: The Edicts of Ashoka record the emperor's conversion to Buddhism and his dhamma policy after the Kalinga war.
interpretation_note: Ashoka's own inscriptions are near-contemporary and among the most reliable sources for ancient India.

claim: The Maurya polity under Ashoka is documented in the major rock edicts as a centrally administered dhamma-ruled state.
interpretation_note: Edicts provide internal administration detail; Greek accounts (Strabo/Megasthenes) corroborate scale.

claim: Ashoka's own edicts (Rock Edict XIII) reference the conquest of Kalinga and its remorse-driven reform.
notes: Real relationship pair verified in ancient_india_example.json.
interpretation_note: First-person royal source; the causal link to dhamma policy is widely accepted.

claim: The Pauline epistles attest to the early Jesus movement and its spread to Antioch.
Paul's letters describe his role in founding early churches across the eastern Mediterranean.
notes: Real relationship pair verified in early_christianity_example.json.

claim: Pliny's Natural History catalogues Egyptian antiquities and mummification practices known to the Roman world.
Strabo's Geographica places Plato's Academy within the suburban deme of Kolonos, near Athens.
Strabo records Socrates' habitual dialogue in the Athenian agora.
Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya dynasty c. 322 BCE with the counsel of Chanakya, per the Arthashastra tradition and later Greek accounts (Megasthenes/Strabo).
interpretation_note: Founding date debated (c. 322 vs 320 BCE); lineage transmitted by later Sanskrit tradition.

claim: Pataliputra (modern Patna) was the Mauryan capital at the Ganges-Son confluence, attested by Megasthenes' Indica (via Strabo) and the Ashokan edicts.
interpretation_note: Site identification with Patna is secure from both literary and epigraphic evidence.

claim: Buddhism arose from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama (5th-4th c. BCE); the Tipitaka preserves the earliest doctrinal corpus.
interpretation_note: Core historicity of the Buddha widely accepted; specific biographical details vary by tradition.

claim: Siddhartha Gautama, the historical Buddha, lived c. 563-483 BCE (traditional); the earliest biographical material is in the Pali Canon.
interpretation_note: Chronology varies across Buddhist traditions; c. 5th-4th c. BCE is the mainstream scholarly range.

claim: The Indus Valley was the heartland of the early Indus (Harappan) Civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE) in modern Pakistan, later integrated into the wider Indic cultural sphere.
interpretation_note: Harappan script remains undeciphered; language attribution unknown.

claim: The Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) was a pivotal conquest by Ashoka, after which he adopted dhamma; attested by Ashokan Major Rock Edict XIII.
interpretation_note: Ashoka's own edict is the primary, near-contemporary source.

claim: Dharma is the central ethical/cosmic concept in Indian thought, promulgated by Ashoka as 'dhamma' in his edicts.
interpretation_note: Ashoka's dhamma was a pragmatic, non-sectarian ethical policy rather than a single doctrinal system.

claim: The Maurya Era (c. 322-185 BCE) was the age of the first Indian empire and its Buddhist flowering, documented by the Ashokan edicts.
interpretation_note: End date (c. 185 BCE, Pushyamitra Shunga) is standard periodization.

claim: The Gupta Period (c. 320-550 CE) was a classical age of India under the Gupta dynasty, famed for Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa) and mathematics (Aryabhata).
interpretation_note: Often termed a 'classical age'; dates approximate.

claim: Kalidasa was a classical Sanskrit poet and playwright of the Gupta court (c. 4th-5th c. CE), author of Abhijnanashakuntalam.
interpretation_note: Exact dates and even historicity debates exist; standard attribution to the Gupta court.

claim: The place-value numeral system with zero was formalized in Gupta-era India; attested by Aryabhata's notation and later inscriptions (e.g., Gwalior).
interpretation_note: Concept of zero as a numeral (shunya) is distinctly Indian; earlier Mesopotamian/Egyptian null-markers differ.

claim: Aryabhata (b. 476 CE) authored the Aryabhatiya, introducing place-value notation, trigonometric functions, and a heliocentric-leaning model.
interpretation_note: Aryabhata's birthplace is traditionally given as Kusumapura (near Pataliputra).

claim: Buddhism spread from India to Central Asia and Han China along the Silk Road from the 2nd c. BCE, carried by monks and merchants.
interpretation_note: Archaeological (e.g., Bamiyan, Dunhuang) and textual evidence corroborate the transmission.

claim: The Maurya polity had indirect awareness of Persian (Achaemenid) administration via the Arthashastra's references; direct contemporaneity was limited (Achaemenid fell 330 BCE).
interpretation_note: Relationship is loose/indirect; included to mark cross-topic awareness, not a strong historical linkage.

claim: The Roman Empire (principate) is conventionally dated from 27 BCE under Augustus and lasted in the West until 476 CE.
interpretation_note: Western fall 476 CE is conventional; Eastern continuation persisted to 1453 CE.

claim: At its height Rome controlled the Mediterranean basin and large parts of Europe, North Africa, and the Near East.
Augustus (born Gaius Octavius, 63 BCE) became the first Roman emperor in 27 BCE after the civil wars.
interpretation_note: Octavian's exact birth name and the nature of the principate are well documented by Tacitus and Suetonius.

claim: Augustus reformed provincial administration and the military, founding the principate system.
The Roman Empire was formally established in 27 BCE when the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus.
Rome is traditionally dated to a founding in 753 BCE, though archaeological evidence places early Rome in the 8th-7th c. BCE.
interpretation_note: The 753 BCE (Ab urbe condita) date is a later antiquarian tradition (Varro); material culture suggests a gradually growing Latin settlement, not a single founding event.

claim: The year 27 BCE marks the traditional beginning of the Roman Empire (principate).
Roman Egypt (Aegyptus) was established as a province in 30 BCE after Octavian's defeat of Cleopatra VII.
Egypt under Rome supplied grain to the capital and was a personal domain of the emperor.
The Byzantine Empire, the eastern continuation of Rome, is conventionally dated from 330 CE (Constantinople's dedication) or 395 CE (formal dominion split).
interpretation_note: Scholars differ on the start date; 330 CE (New Rome) and 395 CE (division) are both used.

claim: Byzantium preserved Roman law (Corpus Juris Civilis) and Greek learning after the West fell in 476 CE.
Christianity emerged in the 1st c. CE within the Roman Judean province and spread across the empire.
Christianity became the state religion of the Roman Empire under Theodosius I (Edict of Thessalonica, 380 CE).
The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE) preceded the empire; its fall followed the civil wars of the 1st c. BCE.
Constantine the Great (r. 306-337 CE) legalized Christianity via the Edict of Milan (313 CE).
Constantine founded Constantinople as the new imperial capital, dedicated in 330 CE.
Julius Caesar (100-44 BCE) crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, precipitating the civil war that ended the Republic.
Caesar was appointed dictator perpetuo in 44 BCE and was assassinated that year.
Constantinople, founded on the site of Byzantium, became the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire.
The Edict of Milan (313 CE) granted Christians legal toleration throughout the Roman Empire.
Augustus (Octavian) was the central actor in the establishment of the Roman Empire in 27 BCE.
The founding event of 27 BCE marks the beginning of the Roman civ-empire entity.
The Roman Empire was established and centered at Rome.
The empire's establishment is dated to 27 BCE (tp-27bc).
Roman Egypt (Aegyptus) was an imperial province administered from Rome.
Roman culture was deeply influenced by Hellenistic Greek art, literature, and philosophy.
The Roman Empire traded indirectly with the eastern Silk Road networks, importing silk and spices via Parthian and later Sassanian intermediaries.
interpretation_note: Direct Rome-Silk Road trade was limited; most exchange was mediated by Parthia/Persia. Roman silk imports are well attested archaeologically.

claim: Rome conquered the Hellenistic Greek world in the Macedonian Wars (ending 146 BCE).
The Byzantine Empire inherited Roman law, administration, and imperial ideology.
Christianity became the predominant religion practiced within the Roman Empire from the 4th c. CE.
Roman/early Christianity carried forward monotheistic tradition rooted in Jewish and Egyptian monotheistic ideas.
The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE) preceded the imperial era beginning in 27 BCE.
The Byzantine Empire succeeded the Western Roman Empire in time (after 476 CE in the West).
Byzantium explicitly styled itself as the continuation of the Roman Empire (translatio imperii).
Constantine ruled from and founded Constantinople as his capital.
Constantine issued (with Licinius) the Edict of Milan in 313 CE.
The Edict of Milan granted Christians toleration, advancing Christianity's status in the empire.
Christianity spread from its Judean origins into a broader early church across the Roman world.
Julius Caesar's actions (dictatorship, 49-44 BCE) precipitated the fall of the Republic that led to the Empire's establishment under Augustus; Caesar himself did not found the Empire.
interpretation_note: Caesar died in 44 BCE, 17 years before the 27 BCE settlement. The relationship is causal/indirect: his assassination triggered the final civil war won by Octavian. Treating Caesar as a direct founder of the Empire is a common simplification.

claim: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from Rome as its first emperor.
